rv.q: It worries so much about keeping you entertained it barely leaves a mark.

But no matter how much of a nerd you are for international cooperation and eco activism, this play by Joe Murphy and Joe Robertson labors in vain to fashion art from meetings mired in the language of bureaucratic minutiae.
That makes Kyoto, Joe Murphy and Joe Robertson's electrifying political thriller about climate diplomacy in the 1990s, an impressive feat.

rv.q: In the skilled hands of co-directors Stephen Daldry and Justin Martin, a complex scientific and historical topic has been transformed into a riveting runaway thriller.
It is fast-paced, loaded with information, and a true ensemble vehicle that uses each inch of designer Miriam Buether’s set to bring audience members closer to the action.

While Kyoto offers striking scenes and moments, often staged at a quick clip by its directors, the play remains a weighty work that’s not always engrossing in spite of the excellence of its actors, who do plenty of heavy lifting to keep it moving along.
Otherwise, watching these debates about climate over a conference table is about as riveting as watching anything that goes on at the United Nations.
A remarkable work, not to be missed!

cn.t: Critics are divided on this climate change docudrama: some praise its urgent, immersive approach to a vital topic, while others find it dramatically inert despite strong production values and good intentions.
